title: Capacities of the 4D superball
W: Viterbo's conjecture that all symplectic capacities agree on convex bodies is false in general, but the known counterexample is not centrally symmetric. On the 4D ball x1^4+y1^4+x2^4+y2^4 <= 1 the cylindrical and Ekeland-Hofer-Zehnder capacities are both known to equal 4Gamma(5/4)^2/Gamma(3/2). Does the largest symplectically embedded round ball have the same capacity?
M: Let $U=\{x_1^4+y_1^4+x_2^4+y_2^4\le1\}\subset(\mathbb R^4,dx_1\wedge dy_1+dx_2\wedge dy_2)$. It is known that $c_{EHZ}(U)=c_Z(U)=c_0:=4\Gamma(5/4)^2/\Gamma(3/2)\approx3.708$. Decide whether the Gromov width $c_G(U)=\sup\{\pi r^2: B^4(r)\hookrightarrow U\text{ symplectically}\}$ equals $c_0$.
why: After Haim-Kislev and Ostrover disproved Viterbo's conjecture, it is open whether all normalized capacities still agree on centrally symmetric convex bodies. The l^4 ball is the simplest centrally symmetric, non-toric convex body whose EHZ and cylindrical capacities are known exactly, so its Gromov width is the sharpest remaining test: a strict inequality would give a centrally symmetric counterexample to strong Viterbo.
diagnosis: A single-instance test case. The structural version, whether all capacities agree on centrally symmetric convex bodies, is already posed openly (Haim-Kislev-Ostrover, Chaidez-Tanny Q.22/26), so generalizing would restate a known open question.
what_changed: Nothing. Confirmed that 2609.37794 gives only c_EHZ=c_Z for l^p balls and no Gromov width. Chaidez-Tanny (2610.31906) prove Viterbo under quaternion-group symmetry but do not treat l^p balls.

title: Cross-polytopes in 4D
W: Every smooth convex body in 4-space should have the eight corners of a regular cross-polytope lying on its boundary.
M: Prove that for every smooth convex body $K\subset\mathbb{R}^4$ there is a regular cross-polytope (a similar copy of $\mathrm{conv}\{\pm e_1,\dots,\pm e_4\}$) all of whose 8 vertices lie on $\partial K$.
why: Inscribing regular octahedra and cross-polytopes (Klee-Wagon Problem 11.5) is a high-dimensional cousin of the square peg problem. Karasev settled every odd prime power dimension with equivariant topology, but the method fails in even dimensions. Dimension 4 is the first open case and needs a genuinely new obstruction computation.
diagnosis: This is the first open case of the known all-dimensions conjecture on inscribing regular cross-polytopes (Makeev; Klee-Wagon 11.5), and Karasev already identifies even dimensions as the gap. Generalizing just restates the posed conjecture, and d=4 alone is a narrow case with low novelty.
what_changed: Nothing. Checked Karasev 0905.2671: odd prime powers only. Found no d=4 result.

title: A monotile that forces quasicrystalline symmetry
W: Every aperiodic monotile known (Socolar-Taylor, the hat, the spectre, and the 3D examples) has tilings with only crystallographic rotational structure: 2-, 3-, 4- or 6-fold. Is there a single tile in the plane whose tilings are all forced to be quasicrystalline with fivefold symmetry, as Penrose tilings are? Or is non-crystallographic symmetry something only two or more tiles can enforce?
M: Call a compact set $T\subset\mathbb R^2$ homeomorphic to a closed disc a monotile if it tiles $\mathbb R^2$ by isometric copies, reflections allowed. For a tiling $\mathcal T$ let $\Omega(\mathcal T)$ be its translation hull in the local topology. Does there exist a monotile $T$ such that for every tiling $\mathcal T$ by copies of $T$, $\Omega(\mathcal T)$ is invariant under rotation by $2\pi/5$ about the origin? (Equivalently up to orientation conventions, every tiling has the same 5-fold rotationally invariant local-isomorphism class.) The analogous question in $\mathbb R^3$, with an icosahedral group $A_5$ in place of $C_5$, is a secondary target.
why: Penrose and Ammann showed that non-crystallographic order can be forced locally with two tiles, and the Einstein problem has now been solved for crystallographic-type hulls. It is open whether one tile with no markings suffices to force the symmetry seen in real quasicrystals. Gummelt's decagon does this only with overlaps (a covering, not a tiling). A positive answer would make the single-tile quasicrystal model of Steinhardt-Jeong exact, and a negative answer would be a new rigidity phenomenon separating one tile from two.
diagnosis: The 3D icosahedral version is an arbitrary harder instance. The reviewer notes the 2D fivefold analogue is open and more natural, but the original framed it as a mere first step.
what_changed: Moved to the plane with 5-fold hull symmetry, which is the canonical non-crystallographic case and directly answers 'can one tile force Penrose-type order?'. Disc topology and no markings keep it honest, and the 3D icosahedral version is kept as secondary.

title: Translative Lebesgue covering
W: Find the convex shape of least area that contains a translated copy of every planar set of diameter 1, when only translations (no rotations or reflections) are allowed. Is the Jung disc of radius 1/sqrt(3), which is optimal for perimeter, also optimal for area?
M: Let $\mathcal D$ be the family of planar sets of diameter at most $1$. Determine $\alpha=\min\{\mathrm{area}(K): K\subset\mathbb R^2 \text{ convex},\ \forall X\in\mathcal D\ \exists t\in\mathbb R^2: X+t\subseteq K\}$ and all minimisers up to translation. In particular decide whether $\alpha<\pi/3$ (the area of the disc of radius $1/\sqrt3$).
why: Lebesgue's universal-cover problem (rigid motions allowed) is a century old and still unsolved; the translation-only version is the natural rigid analogue of Pal's solution of the convex Kakeya problem (equilateral triangle of height 1) and of Bezdek-Connelly's theorem that the disc of radius 1/sqrt3 is the unique minimum-perimeter translation cover of diameter-1 sets. Its answer measures how much rotation actually helps in Lebesgue's problem.
diagnosis: This is already posed: Bezdek-Connelly (1989) list the minimum-area translation cover for diameter-1 sets as unknown, so novelty is low. It is a natural classical covering question, but a narrow niche cousin of Lebesgue's problem.
what_changed: Nothing in substance. It is already in its canonical form and has no better general version. Its prior posing should be credited to Bezdek-Connelly, Amer. Math. Monthly 1989.

title: Information-tight sorting of pattern classes
W: An array is promised to avoid a fixed pattern. Counting the allowed orders gives a lower bound on the comparisons needed to sort it, and Fredman's theorem says this bound plus 2n always suffices. Opler (2024) showed the right order of magnitude is linear. Is the counting bound tight up to lower-order terms, o(n), for every pattern?
M: For a permutation $\tau$ let $C_\tau(n)$ be the minimum worst-case number of comparisons of a decision tree that sorts $a_1,\dots,a_n$ under the promise that their order pattern lies in $\mathrm{Av}_n(\tau)$. Fredman: $\log_2|\mathrm{Av}_n(\tau)|\le C_\tau(n)\le\log_2|\mathrm{Av}_n(\tau)|+2n$. Decide whether $C_\tau(n)=\log_2|\mathrm{Av}_n(\tau)|+o(n)$ for every $\tau$, and in particular for $\tau=1324$.
why: The comparison model is one of the few settings where information-theoretic lower bounds are often nearly exact. Even for unrestricted sorting it is unknown whether $\log_2 n!+o(n)$ comparisons suffice. Pattern classes give a family where this question is harder to dismiss. A linear gap for some $\tau$ would need a new lower-bound technique, and tightness for every $\tau$ would need a strong structural sorting algorithm.
diagnosis: A clean but niche additive-term question. Opler only settles constant factors. Linear gaps do occur for some non-principal classes (see below), so the principal Av(tau) case is sharper but still narrow.
what_changed: Unchanged. A new check found that Av(231,312,321) (disjoint adjacent swaps, |C_n|=F_{n+1}) needs n-1 comparisons by an adversary argument, against log2 F_{n+1}≈0.694n. So the statement must stay restricted to single patterns.

title: Jacobi matrix of primes
W: Build an infinite tridiagonal (Jacobi) matrix with zero diagonal and the primes 2, 3, 5, 7, ... on the off-diagonals. The standard criteria for purely absolutely continuous spectrum need the off-diagonal sequence to vary regularly, and they just fail because prime gaps fluctuate. Decide whether the spectrum is nevertheless purely absolutely continuous on the whole real line.
M: Let $J$ be the self-adjoint Jacobi operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ given by $(Ju)_n=p_{n-1}u_{n-1}+p_nu_{n+1}$ (with $p_0u_0:=0$), where $p_n$ is the $n$-th prime. It is self-adjoint by Carleman's criterion, since $\sum1/p_n=\infty$. Decide whether $\sigma(J)=\sigma_{ac}(J)=\mathbb R$ with no singular part.
why: Unbounded Jacobi matrices with weights $a_n\to\infty$ and $b_n=0$ have purely absolutely continuous spectrum under bounded-variation conditions on $a_{n+1}/a_n$ (Janas-Naboko, Clark). For the primes, the variation of $p_{n+1}/p_n$ diverges like $\sum g_n/p_n$. A Prüfer heuristic suggests the real obstruction is the oscillatory series $\sum(-1)^n g_n/p_n\,e^{i\phi_n}$ ($g_n$ the prime gaps), so the spectral type appears to encode a parity-of-index statistic of prime gaps.
diagnosis: This is one arbitrary arithmetic instance. The claimed obstruction is a parity-of-index statistic of prime gaps, which likely needs unproven gap estimates, so the problem works as a benchmark more than a theory question. No natural family generalizes it without becoming a standard Jacobi-matrix question.
what_changed: Nothing. A literature search (Jacobi matrices with prime weights, Janas-Naboko-type criteria) found no treatment of this matrix. The statement stays as is.

title: Mass-critical scattering on flat cones
W: Dodson proved that the defocusing cubic Schrodinger equation in the plane scatters for every finite-mass initial state. Prove the same on every flat cone, a plane with a single conical singularity of total angle alpha. For alpha = 2pi/k it follows from Dodson by symmetry, and radial data are also easy. Every other angle, such as the surface of a cube corner (alpha = 3pi/2) or alpha > 2pi, is open.
M: For $\alpha>0$ let $\mathcal C_\alpha=(0,\infty)\times(\mathbb R/\alpha\mathbb Z)$ with metric $dr^2+r^2d\theta^2$ and $\Delta$ the Friedrichs extension of the Laplacian on $C_c^\infty(\mathcal C_\alpha)$. Prove that for every $\alpha>0$ and every $u_0\in L^2(\mathcal C_\alpha)$ the solution of $iu_t+\Delta u=|u|^2u$, $u(0)=u_0$, is global with $\|u\|_{L^4_{t,x}(\mathbb R\times\mathcal C_\alpha)}<\infty$, hence scatters in $L^2$. (Known: $\alpha=2\pi/k$, since $\mathcal C_{2\pi/k}=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z_k$ and Dodson applies to $\mathbb Z_k$-invariant data. Radial data for any $\alpha$, since the radial equation coincides with the 2D one.)
why: Dodson's theorem uses Euclidean translation and Galilean symmetry. On a cone with angle not of the form 2pi/k, translations and Galilean boosts are lost, waves diffract at the apex, and concentration at the apex rescales back to the same cone. The flat-cone family is the simplest geometry testing whether concentration-compactness and rigidity survive a genuine singularity at the mass-critical level. Known results on cones (Zhang-Zheng, Blair-Ford-Marzuola) give only small data or energy-space results.
diagnosis: The angle 3pi/2 was cosmetic and the trivial cases were not identified, so the problem read as an isolated instance with no literature check.
what_changed: Extended to all cone angles. Identified the solved cases: alpha=2pi/k by the quotient R^2/Z_k, and radial data. The open set is now exactly the non-quotient angles. Literature check found only small-data or H^1 results on cones.

title: Charge on a Fermat conductor
W: Put a unit of electric charge on a perfectly conducting solid x^4+y^4+z^4 <= 1. Show that the surface charge is thinnest exactly at the six flat points (+-1,0,0),... and thickest exactly at the eight points in the diagonal directions.
M: Let $K=\{x^4+y^4+z^4\le1\}\subset\mathbb R^3$ and let $\mu=\rho\,d\sigma$ be its Newtonian (capacitary) equilibrium measure, $\sigma$ surface measure on $\partial K$ ($\rho$ is real-analytic and positive since $\partial K$ is analytic). Prove that $\min_{\partial K}\rho$ is attained exactly at $(\pm1,0,0),(0,\pm1,0),(0,0,\pm1)$ and $\max_{\partial K}\rho$ exactly at $3^{-1/4}(\pm1,\pm1,\pm1)$.
why: It is folklore that charge accumulates where a conductor is more curved, but the density is nonlocal and only exactly known for ellipsoids (where it is proportional to K^{1/4}). The Fermat superball is the simplest smooth convex body that is not an ellipsoid and has flat points; here Gaussian curvature K=9x^2y^2z^2/(x^6+y^6+z^6)^2 even vanishes along three whole great curves, so rho cannot be a function of K, and a proof needs a genuinely nonlocal comparison argument.
diagnosis: The general form ('density is maximized where curvature is') looks false. Heuristically, a cube with edge rounding delta and corner rounding delta^0.7 gives an edge density of about delta^(-1/3) against a corner density of about delta^(-0.38). That leaves only a symmetric special instance.
what_changed: Nothing. The checked literature (Liu-type K^{1/4} laws, which are known to fail beyond quadrics) has no extremal-point theorem for superballs. The structural generalization breaks, so the problem stays a narrow instance.

title: Irrationality of the quartic oscillator ground state
W: The lowest energy of the quartic oscillator, -d^2/dx^2 + x^4 on the line, is about 1.0603620905. Show that it is irrational.
M: Let $E_0=\min\sigma\big(-\tfrac{d^2}{dx^2}+x^4\big)$, the operator taken self-adjoint on $L^2(\mathbb R)$ ($E_0=1.06036209048418\ldots$). Prove that $E_0\notin\mathbb Q$.
why: Irrationality and transcendence are known for spectral data of exactly solvable problems, such as Bessel zeros via Siegel's theorem. For a genuinely non-solvable Schrödinger operator, apparently nothing is known. Voros's exact WKB and spectral-determinant functional relations describe E_0 implicitly, so a proof would have to turn those relations, or a series or continued fraction for E_0, into Diophantine information.
diagnosis: An isolated 'benchmark of ignorance' with no attack route. The choice of x^4 and E_0 is arbitrary, and natural generalizations (any eigenvalue, any non-solvable polynomial potential) are equally hopeless and add no structure.
what_changed: Nothing. A search found no work on the arithmetic nature of anharmonic eigenvalues.
